cooling_items.text:
The building is not equipped with a centralized cooling system. Cooling within individual suites is provided by a combination of window-mounted air conditioners and portable indoor air-conditioning units.

These decentralized cooling devices are generally less efficient than modern centralized or heat-pump-based systems. Typical window and portable air-conditioning units operate with relatively low coefficients of performance (COP), often below 3.0, compared to high-efficiency heat pump systems which can achieve COP values exceeding 4.5–5.0 under favorable conditions.

In addition to reduced cooling efficiency, window-mounted air-conditioning units can negatively impact building envelope performance. Improper sealing around window installations may allow uncontrolled air infiltration during the heating season, increasing heat loss, draft complaints, and overall space-heating energy consumption. Installation of a air source heat pump (ASHP) system could be considered in a short term to mid term.

measures.existing_conditions: The existing HVAC mechanical systems—including MUAs, exhaust fans, heating boilers, DHW plant, cooling equipment, and pumps—are controlled manually or via basic local thermostats and temperature sensors. There is minimal outdoor-air reset, limited boiler sequencing, and no centralized scheduling or monitoring. Equipment often operates during unoccupied periods, leading to excessive energy use and chronic overheating.
measures.measure_title: Install New Building Automation System (BAS)
measures.notes: Install a new central BAS to Control boilers, DHW, MUAs, pumps and exhaust fans with scheduling, reset and remote access, reducing energy use and maintenance. Improve building operation and management.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to install a centralized BAS to control all major HVAC systems. The BAS would provide occupancy-based scheduling, outdoor-temperature reset for boilers, zone-level temperature modulation, real-time monitoring, remote access, and alarm notifications. Improved control will reduce unnecessary run time, lower energy consumption, and improve comfort while reducing maintenance costs through better diagnostics. Utility incentives for advanced building controls can further improve project economics, with typical paybacks on the order of 3–4 years.

measures.existing_conditions:
The building is currently served by a heating-only hydronic distribution system. Space heating is provided through copper-fin baseboard heaters and hydronic radiators supplied by a centralized boiler plant located in the main mechanical room.

The building does not have a central cooling system. No in-suite fan coil units, chillers, or centralized cooling infrastructure are present. As a result, suite-level cooling, where provided, relies on window A/C or portable air-conditioning units. These localized cooling devices typically operate independently, are relatively inefficient, and contribute to increased electrical demand during the cooling season.
measures.measure_title: Transition Baseboard Heater to Mini-Split Heat Pump Systems
measures.notes: Replace current system with air-source heat pumps, allowing simultaneous heating and cooling.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the existing hydronic baseboard heating systems with mini-split air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems to provide both space heating and cooling at the suite level.

The existing hydronic baseboard system relies on centrally generated hot water distributed throughout the building. While functional for heating, this system provides heating only, operates at relatively high distribution temperatures, and does not provide cooling. In addition, system efficiency is constrained by boiler plant performance, distribution losses, and limited zone-level control.

In contrast, mini-split heat pump systems typically operate at a COP of approximately 3 to 4 under suitable operating conditions, allowing them to deliver three to four units of heat for each unit of electrical energy consumed by transferring heat from the outdoor air to the indoor space. This results in a substantial reduction in energy consumption while maintaining or improving occupant comfort.

In addition to improved heating efficiency, the proposed mini-split systems would introduce dedicated cooling capability to the suites. This would eliminate the need for separate window-mounted or portable air-conditioning units, improving overall system efficiency, reducing peak electrical demand, and simplifying long-term maintenance.

The proposed upgrade would transition the building from an aging, single-function heating system to a modern, high-efficiency heating and cooling solution, improving occupant comfort, operational performance, and long-term energy efficiency.

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to be carried out at the next project stage or as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit. The feasibility assessment should consider the available electrical service capacity, potential electrical infrastructure upgrades, and system integration constraints. It is also recommended that the existing hydronic heating system be retained as a backup system to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: The existing piping arrangement separates the space-heating and domestic hot water (DHW) systems into independent loops. The space-heating system operates with a primary distribution loop serving building loads, while the DHW system is served by a dedicated boiler loop with separate circulation. This configuration can limit system-level temperature coordination between heating and DHW loads and may contribute to inefficient boiler operation during part-load or shoulder-season conditions.
measures.measure_title: Primary–Secondary Boiler and DHW Piping Reconfiguration
measures.notes: Reconfigure heating and DHW piping to a primary–secondary layout, hydraulically separating loops to improve temperature control, boiler protection and plant efficiency.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to reconfigure the heating and DHW piping into a Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. In a P-S design, the boiler primary loop circulates hot water while secondary loops draw only the flow required for each load, including space heating zones and DHW generation.

This configuration provides hydraulic separation between the boiler plant and building loads, improves system stability during varying load conditions, and enables more effective outdoor-air temperature reset strategies and control optimization.

With improved hydraulic separation, future system upgrades such as enhanced DHW generation strategies or alternative DHW configurations may also become feasible. When combined with a condensing boiler retrofit, the boiler plant may potentially be optimized in size and staging strategy, reducing capital and long-term maintenance costs.. Further engineering review is required to finalize the detailed design.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: The domestic hot water (DHW) system is currently served by an atmospheric gas-fired boiler that is near or past the end of its typical service life. Atmospheric boilers have relatively low thermal efficiency, high standby losses and limited turndown capability. As equipment ages, efficiency and reliability decline and the risk of failure increases.
measures.measure_title: Replace DHW Boiler with Condensing Boiler
measures.notes: Replace atmospheric DHW boiler with a high-efficiency condensing model and optimised piping to lower gas use, increase reliability and improve safety.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to replace the existing atmospheric DHW boiler with a new high-efficiency condensing boiler, typically rated around 95% thermal efficiency. The new boiler would be equipped with fully modulating burners and integrated controls to match output to DHW demand, reducing cycling and standby losses. Piping can be reconfigured to minimize standby heat loss and protect the boiler from thermal shock. This retrofit will improve energy efficiency, enhance reliability and reduce safety concerns associated with aging atmospheric equipment. Additional engineering is required to confirm sizing, venting and integration with the existing DHW system.

measures.existing_conditions:
Windows and exterior doors located on the front façade of the building have been previously replaced and are in generally good condition. In contrast, the rear façade window and door assemblies remain original and were observed to be in poor condition.

The rear windows exhibit signs of frame deterioration, aging seals, and reduced air-tightness. Given the age of the assemblies, the insulating glazing units are likely operating below their original thermal performance due to seal
measures.measure_title: Replacement of Windows and Exterior Doors
measures.notes: Replacement of the original  windows and exterior doors
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended that the rear façade windows and exterior doors be replaced with modern high-performance assemblies. New glazing systems incorporating low-emissivity (low-E) coatings, thermally improved frames, and enhanced seal technology would reduce heat loss and improve overall building envelope performance.

Replacement exterior doors should include insulated cores, continuous weatherstripping, and improved air sealing to minimize infiltration.

Given that the front façade assemblies have already been upgraded, a phased approach targeting only the rear façade is appropriate and cost-effective. This targeted envelope improvement would enhance occupant comfort, reduce uncontrolled air leakage, and lower heating demand while aligning with long-term capital planning objectives.

measures.existing_conditions:
The existing heating boilers in the mechanical room are non-condensing, gas-fired {______ }units installed in {______}, with an estimated thermal efficiency of approximately {_______}%. As non-condensing equipment, they operate with higher flue-gas temperatures and cannot recover latent heat from combustion, resulting in reduced overall efficiency compared to modern condensing boiler technologies.

The boilers also {not integrate with BAS}, lack advanced control features such as setpoint adjustment based on outdoor air temperature and real-time modulation optimization. This limited control capability contributes to frequent short cycling and increased natural gas consumption. As a result, the system experiences elevated utility costs and higher greenhouse gas emissions.

While the boilers remain operational and continue to provide reliable heating performance, their age and conventional atmospheric design limit overall system efficiency compared to modern condensing technology. Although there is no immediate need for replacement, planning for a long-term boiler upgrade would allow the building to benefit from improved energy efficiency, reduced operating costs, and enhanced modulation and control capabilities in future years.
measures.measure_title: Condensing Boiler Retrofit
measures.notes: Replace aging non condensing boilers with high-efficiency condensing units and improved piping to enable true condensing operation, lowering gas consumption improve overall energy efficiency and extending plant life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommended that the existing non-condensing boilers be replaced with high-efficiency condensing boilers. Condensing boilers are designed to extract additional heat from the flue gases by recovering latent heat through a secondary heat exchanger, allowing them to achieve thermal efficiencies of up to 98%. This upgrade would substantially reduce natural gas consumption, lower utility costs, and improve overall system performance.

Modern condensing boilers also provide advanced control capabilities, including high-turndown modulation, integrated sequencing, and seamless compatibility with Building Automation Systems (BAS). These features improve load matching, reduce equipment cycling, and enhance operational reliability.

Upgrading to condensing boiler technology not only increases energy efficiency and reduces ongoing operating costs but also supports long-term sustainability objectives and contributes to meaningful reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. Piping would be reconfigured to reduce standby losses and protect the boilers from thermal shock.

measures.existing_conditions:
The building is served by an aging rooftop supply fan that provides outdoor ventilation air to interior corridors through centralized ductwork. Based on site observations, the unit appears to be original to the building (circa 1970) and shows visible signs of deterioration, including surface corrosion, weather-related wear, and general aging due to prolonged rooftop exposure.
No gas-fired heating section, cooling coil, or integrated conditioning components were observed. As such, the system likely delivers unconditioned outdoor air directly to corridor spaces. 
Due to the lack of airflow modulation and temperature control, the existing ventilation system may contribute to increased building heat loss during winter months and reduced overall ventilation efficiency. The aging supply fan equipment is approaching or exceeding its typical service life and may present reliability concerns in the near term.
measures.measure_title: Aging MUA Hydronic Conversion with BAS and VFDs
measures.notes: Convert gas-fired MUAs to hydronic coils served by a central condensing boiler plant, with BAS control and VFDs to improve ventilation efficiency and reduce gas use.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to replace the existing rooftop supply fan with a new dedicated make-up air unit (MUA) equipped with hydronic heating coils connected to the central boiler plant.
The proposed unit would incorporate:
•	Hydronic heating coil for tempering outdoor ventilation air
•	Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) for supply fan speed control
•	Modulating dampers and improved airflow control
•	Integration with the Building Automation System (BAS)
With BAS integration, the new MUA system could implement supply-air temperature reset, optimized ventilation scheduling, and improved monitoring and alarm capabilities.
Tempering ventilation air using the central boiler plant would reduce the reliance on electric corridor heating and improve overall building heating efficiency. The addition of VFD control would also reduce electrical consumption and mechanical wear by allowing fan operation to match actual ventilation demand.
Upgrading the corridor ventilation system will improve occupant comfort, enhance ventilation control, and support long-term building energy performance.
*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: Based on site observations, existing make-up air (MUA) units are located in proximity to central exhaust fan systems within the mechanical rooms. Exhaust air operates at constant volume and discharges continuously to the exterior. The current configuration does not incorporate heat recovery between exhaust air and incoming outdoor air, resulting in avoidable ventilation-related energy losses during both heating and cooling seasons.
measures.measure_title: Install Heat Recovery (ERV) on Existing MUA System
measures.notes: Assess feasibility of integrating heat recovery (ERV) into existing MUA/exhaust configuration to reduce ventilation energy losses and improve overall system efficiency.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommended to assess the feasibility of installing or upgrading an Energy Recovery Ventilator (ERV) or incorporating heat recovery coils within the existing MUA system. Where exhaust fans are located in close proximity to the MUA, heat recovery may be effectively integrated to transfer thermal energy from exhaust air to incoming fresh air.

The proposed system would install heat recovery coils within the fresh air and exhaust air duct streams, allowing preheating (or precooling) of ventilation air and reducing the heating and cooling load on the mechanical systems.

This measure would reduce ventilation-related energy consumption and improve overall system efficiency. Implementation is not expected to negatively impact occupant comfort, health, or safety relative to existing conditions.

*Further engineering review is required to evaluate duct capacity, fan static pressure availability, physical space constraints, and structural limitations.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:

measures.existing_conditions: At the present, the building relies on external utilities to provide electricity to power the building which might lead to high electrical energy costs.
measures.measure_title: Solar PV : Electricity Generation
measures.notes: Install net metered solar PV generated electricity to offset electricity consumption.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
The current state of the solar industry in Ontario is focused on “net metering” as power export to the grid is no longer an option. Rather than power export, net metered solar facilities use the generated electricity to offset electricity consumption within the facility. Since power export is not feasible, the system should be sized to only meet the baseload energy consumption of the building. This building has a high electrical consumption and ample roof space, which makes it a candidate for solar PV. 

A preliminary study is required to accurately estimate the system cost and savings for a Solar PV system

Upgrading through the Trade‑In Program is recommended to replace outdated units with OCPP‑networked TAR‑M chargers, providing managed access, usage metering, and load balancing. Early participants benefit from reduced capital cost, including no‑cost upgrades for the first two owners, along with ongoing carbon‑credit rebates of $0.03–$0.05/kWh.

Windows and exterior doors located on the front façade of the building have been previously replaced and are in generally good condition. In contrast, the rear façade window and door assemblies remain original and were observed to be in poor condition.

The rear windows exhibit signs of frame deterioration, aging seals, and reduced air-tightness. Given the age of the assemblies, the insulating glazing units are likely operating below their original thermal performance due to seal
measures.measure_title: Replacement of Windows and Exterior Doors
measures.notes: Replacement of the original  windows and exterior doors
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended that the rear façade windows and exterior doors be replaced with modern high-performance assemblies. New glazing systems incorporating low-emissivity (low-E) coatings, thermally improved frames, and enhanced seal technology would reduce heat loss and improve overall building envelope performance.

Replacement exterior doors should include insulated cores, continuous weatherstripping, and improved air sealing to minimize infiltration.

Given that the front façade assemblies have already been upgraded, a phased approach targeting only the rear façade is appropriate and cost-effective. This targeted envelope improvement would enhance occupant comfort, reduce uncontrolled air leakage, and lower heating demand while aligning with long-term capital planning objectives.

measures.existing_conditions:
The existing heating boilers in the mechanical room are non-condensing, gas-fired {______ }units installed in {______}, with an estimated thermal efficiency of approximately {_______}%. As non-condensing equipment, they operate with higher flue-gas temperatures and cannot recover latent heat from combustion, resulting in reduced overall efficiency compared to modern condensing boiler technologies.

The boilers also {not integrate with BAS}, lack advanced control features such as setpoint adjustment based on outdoor air temperature and real-time modulation optimization. This limited control capability contributes to frequent short cycling and increased natural gas consumption. As a result, the system experiences elevated utility costs and higher greenhouse gas emissions.

While the boilers remain operational and continue to provide reliable heating performance, their age and conventional atmospheric design limit overall system efficiency compared to modern condensing technology. Although there is no immediate need for replacement, planning for a long-term boiler upgrade would allow the building to benefit from improved energy efficiency, reduced operating costs, and enhanced modulation and control capabilities in future years.
measures.measure_title: Condensing Boiler Retrofit
measures.notes: Replace aging non condensing boilers with high-efficiency condensing units and improved piping to enable true condensing operation, lowering gas consumption improve overall energy efficiency and extending plant life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommended that the existing non-condensing boilers be replaced with high-efficiency condensing boilers. Condensing boilers are designed to extract additional heat from the flue gases by recovering latent heat through a secondary heat exchanger, allowing them to achieve thermal efficiencies of up to 98%. This upgrade would substantially reduce natural gas consumption, lower utility costs, and improve overall system performance.

Modern condensing boilers also provide advanced control capabilities, including high-turndown modulation, integrated sequencing, and seamless compatibility with Building Automation Systems (BAS). These features improve load matching, reduce equipment cycling, and enhance operational reliability.

Upgrading to condensing boiler technology not only increases energy efficiency and reduces ongoing operating costs but also supports long-term sustainability objectives and contributes to meaningful reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. Piping would be reconfigured to reduce standby losses and protect the boilers from thermal shock.

measures.existing_conditions:
The building is served by an aging rooftop supply fan that provides outdoor ventilation air to interior corridors through centralized ductwork. Based on site observations, the unit appears to be original to the building (circa 1970) and shows visible signs of deterioration, including surface corrosion, weather-related wear, and general aging due to prolonged rooftop exposure.
No gas-fired heating section, cooling coil, or integrated conditioning components were observed. As such, the system likely delivers unconditioned outdoor air directly to corridor spaces. 
Due to the lack of airflow modulation and temperature control, the existing ventilation system may contribute to increased building heat loss during winter months and reduced overall ventilation efficiency. The aging supply fan equipment is approaching or exceeding its typical service life and may present reliability concerns in the near term.
measures.measure_title: Aging MUA Hydronic Conversion with BAS and VFDs
measures.notes: Convert gas-fired MUAs to hydronic coils served by a central condensing boiler plant, with BAS control and VFDs to improve ventilation efficiency and reduce gas use.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to replace the existing rooftop supply fan with a new dedicated make-up air unit (MUA) equipped with hydronic heating coils connected to the central boiler plant.
The proposed unit would incorporate:
•	Hydronic heating coil for tempering outdoor ventilation air
•	Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) for supply fan speed control
•	Modulating dampers and improved airflow control
•	Integration with the Building Automation System (BAS)
With BAS integration, the new MUA system could implement supply-air temperature reset, optimized ventilation scheduling, and improved monitoring and alarm capabilities.
Tempering ventilation air using the central boiler plant would reduce the reliance on electric corridor heating and improve overall building heating efficiency. The addition of VFD control would also reduce electrical consumption and mechanical wear by allowing fan operation to match actual ventilation demand.
Upgrading the corridor ventilation system will improve occupant comfort, enhance ventilation control, and support long-term building energy performance.
*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: Based on site observations, existing make-up air (MUA) units are located in proximity to central exhaust fan systems within the mechanical rooms. Exhaust air operates at constant volume and discharges continuously to the exterior. The current configuration does not incorporate heat recovery between exhaust air and incoming outdoor air, resulting in avoidable ventilation-related energy losses during both heating and cooling seasons.
measures.measure_title: Install Heat Recovery (ERV) on Existing MUA System
measures.notes: Assess feasibility of integrating heat recovery (ERV) into existing MUA/exhaust configuration to reduce ventilation energy losses and improve overall system efficiency.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommended to assess the feasibility of installing or upgrading an Energy Recovery Ventilator (ERV) or incorporating heat recovery coils within the existing MUA system. Where exhaust fans are located in close proximity to the MUA, heat recovery may be effectively integrated to transfer thermal energy from exhaust air to incoming fresh air.

The proposed system would install heat recovery coils within the fresh air and exhaust air duct streams, allowing preheating (or precooling) of ventilation air and reducing the heating and cooling load on the mechanical systems.

This measure would reduce ventilation-related energy consumption and improve overall system efficiency. Implementation is not expected to negatively impact occupant comfort, health, or safety relative to existing conditions.

*Further engineering review is required to evaluate duct capacity, fan static pressure availability, physical space constraints, and structural limitations.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: At the present, the building relies on external utilities to provide electricity to power the building which might lead to high electrical energy costs.
measures.measure_title: Solar PV : Electricity Generation
measures.notes: Install net metered solar PV generated electricity to offset electricity consumption.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
The current state of the solar industry in Ontario is focused on “net metering” as power export to the grid is no longer an option. Rather than power export, net metered solar facilities use the generated electricity to offset electricity consumption within the facility. Since power export is not feasible, the system should be sized to only meet the baseload energy consumption of the building. This building has a high electrical consumption and ample roof space, which makes it a candidate for solar PV. 

A preliminary study is required to accurately estimate the system cost and savings for a Solar PV system

measures.existing_conditions: Electric vehicle (EV) ownership is expected to grow substantially over the next decade, and many multi-residential and commercial buildings currently lack dedicated EV charging infrastructure for residents, staff, or visitors
measures.measure_title: EV Charging Stations
measures.notes: Plan and install EV charging infrastructure for residents and staff, contact us for more detail.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Upgrading through the Trade‑In Program is recommended to replace outdated units with OCPP‑networked TAR‑M chargers, providing managed access, usage metering, and load balancing. Early participants benefit from reduced capital cost, including no‑cost upgrades for the first two owners, along with ongoing carbon‑credit rebates of $0.03–$0.05/kWh.

*Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/

misc_items.text: The building envelope appears to be in generally good condition, with no significant signs of air leakage or deterioration observed at the time of the site visit. Envelope components appear to be performing as intended.
misc_items.title: Envelope Condition (Good)

misc_items.text: Lighting throughout the building is generally in good working order. Common areas, corridors, and service spaces appear to be equipped with a mix of LED and fluorescent fixtures. No widespread outages were observed during the walkthrough, and the overall lighting levels were appropriate for the building’s use. Further savings may be available through continued LED retrofit and the use of occupancy-based controls in selected low-traffic areas. Or installing light control in the parking area.
misc_items.title: Lighting condition and controls

misc_items.text: In aging buildings, even double-pane window assemblies may experience gradual deterioration of glazing seals over time. Loss of insulating gas or degradation of the sealed air space between panes can reduce overall thermal performance. While the existing windows were observed to be in generally fair condition, it would be prudent to incorporate sealant renewal and eventual glazing upgrades into the building’s long-term capital planning strategy.
misc_items.title: Window condition (Aging double pane)

misc_items.text: Suite temperatures are regulated through boiler-room setpoints and/or manual adjustments at the central plant, resulting in limited ability to respond to variations in occupancy, solar gains, or individual comfort preferences. This centralized control approach may contribute to overheating in some suites and underheating in others, increasing overall heating energy consumption and occupant complaints.
misc_items.title: No Insuite Thermostat

misc_items.text: General maintenance observations include isolated leakage at mechanical fittings and signs of aging insulation in select areas. Continued preventive maintenance and timely repair of minor leaks will help preserve system performance and avoid escalation into larger service issues.
misc_items.title: Leakage and maintenance notes

ventilation_items.text:
The building is equipped with a rooftop supply fan that provides ventilation air to the interior corridor spaces through centralized ductwork. Based on site observations, the unit appears to be original to the building (circa 1970) and shows visible signs of aging, including surface corrosion, weather-related deterioration, and general wear due to prolonged rooftop exposure.

No visible gas-fired heating section, cooling coil, or integrated conditioning components were observed during the assessment. As such, the system likely delivers unconditioned outdoor air to the corridors. Heating of common spaces rely on electric radiators.

Overall, the rooftop supply fan is considered to be in poor to fair condition due to age and exposure. While functional at the time of inspection, the equipment is approaching or exceeding its typical service life and should be evaluated for replacement in the short to medium term to ensure reliable ventilation performance.
